title: Long Last Love
program_note:
Long Last Love, written for Kay Kyurim Rhie and Chris Kim on the occasion of the marriage, employs two traditional Korean melodies: Kkok Du Gak Ssi, and Mok Ryun Hwa. The first of these, Kkok Du Gak Ssi, is from a children’s puppet theater tale, and tells the story of a bride who, ultimately, runs away to avoid marrying her betrothed. In the music, however, this tune, having emerged as from a memory, is eclipsed by the second tune, Mok Ryun Hwa, which compares the singer’s lover to a magnolia. In the end, the children’s tune is banished back to the status of distant memory, as true love triumphs over childhood fears.

A Note on the Compositional Technique. Like much of my recent music, this composition mixes diatonic with “atonal” music. Here, in addition to the two Korean tunes, there is a rising or falling series of notes based upon a simple arithmetic sequence (half-step, whole-step, minor-third, major-third, perfect fourth, etc.). This arithmetic sequence itself produces minor seventh chords, together with minor-second and tritone dissonances. The minor seventh chords, in turn, form the basis of the pentatonicism of the principal diatonic material—that is, the two different Korean folk songs. The two songs and the sequence are mixed together in a way which will, I hope, enrich each of the other elements while not detracting from their own inherent beauty.

David S. Lefkowitz

Los Angeles, CA

June, 2005
